subject: Behavioral Economics
title: Who Decides What's Best?
description: A 60-second lesson on Who Decides What's Best?.

hook.text: Nudging people to save more assumes saving is better. But what if someone needs money now for medical bills?

buildup.text: The 'as judged by themselves' criterion from Thaler and Sunstein says a nudge is justified only if people would agree.

discovery.text: But present-self and future-self often disagree. Present-you wants cake. Future-you wants health.

twist.text: Cultural values differ. A savings nudge in one country might clash with gift-giving norms in another.

climax.text: Ethical nudging requires humility. Test, measure, and respect opt-outs. The nudger must be accountable for outcomes.

punchline.text: Design for the people, not for the designer.

quiz.question: What is the 'as judged by themselves' criterion?
options: Experts always know what's best for people
A nudge is justified only if people would agree it benefits them

details.summary: The question of who decides what is best goes to the heart of nudge ethics. Choice architects make implicit value judgments about which outcomes are desirable when they design defaults and frames.
details.whyItMatters: Every nudge embodies a value judgment about what constitutes a better outcome. Who has the authority to make this judgment, and whether they can make it well for diverse populations, determines the legitimacy and fairness of the entire nudge.
takeaways: Every nudge implies a judgment about which option is better for the chooser
Democratic oversight and transparency help legitimize value judgments in nudge design
Heterogeneous populations make one-size-fits-all judgments about what is best problematic

faq.question: How do choice architects decide what is best for diverse populations?
faq.answer: The standard is what a fully informed, deliberate person would choose for themselves. But preferences vary across individuals. Choice architects use empirical research, democratic deliberation, and transparent reasoning.

faq.question: What safeguards prevent choice architects from abusing their power?
faq.answer: Transparency about nudge design and goals. Democratic oversight through elected officials. Rigorous testing through randomized trials. Easy opt-out that preserves genuine freedom. Public debate about which nudges are legitimate. These safeguards constrain the power inherent in choice architecture.
